title: Vacuum and ejectors
ends: Leaks hide when they see you coming.

steps.q: At sea level, the vacuum gauge reads −740 mmHg. What is the absolute pressure?
steps.title: Gauge vs absolute
steps.summary: A vacuum gauge reads relative to the local atmosphere, about 760 mmHg at sea level. Absolute pressure is atmosphere minus vacuum: 760 − 740 = 20 mmHg absolute, about 27 mbar. At altitude the atmosphere is lower, so the same gauge reading is a different absolute pressure; specify vacuum in absolute units.

steps.q: Isolated from the system, the pump pulls its normal vacuum on the same gauge. Where is the problem?
steps.title: Split the problem
steps.summary: Isolate the vacuum pump from the system and check the vacuum it reaches on its own. If the pump alone reaches its normal vacuum, it is healthy and the problem is upstream: either air leaking into the system, or a vapour load from wet product, solvent in the lines or a warm condenser.

opts.t: In the system: a leak or a vapour load

steps.q: You isolate the system and watch the pressure rise. How do you tell a leak from vapour?
board: How do you tell a leak
steps.title: Rate of rise
steps.summary: Pull the system down, isolate it and log the pressure every minute. Air leaking in arrives at a steady rate, so the pressure rises in a straight line. Vapour from the contents stops once the space reaches the vapour pressure, so the curve flattens. At about 20 °C the air leak in kg/h is about 0.07 × volume (m³) × pressure rise (mbar/min); a 2 m³ system rising 10 mbar in 10 minutes takes in about 0.14 kg/h of air.

opts.t: A leak rises in a straight line; vapour levels off
A leak levels off; vapour keeps rising

steps.q: The motive steam pressure to an ejector falls below design. What happens?
steps.title: Ejector breaks
steps.summary: A steam ejector has no moving parts: motive steam through a nozzle entrains gas from the suction and compresses the mixture to the discharge pressure. It needs its full design steam pressure to do that. Below design, an ejector does not weaken gradually; it breaks and the vacuum falls off suddenly. Keep motive steam at or slightly above design pressure, and dry, since wet steam erodes the nozzle.

draw: steam P at or above design

steps.q: Summer. The inter-condenser cooling water runs warmer. What happens to a two-stage ejector?
steps.title: Summer vacuum
steps.summary: In a two-stage ejector, the inter-condenser condenses steam and vapour from the first stage so the second stage only handles the remainder. Warmer cooling water condenses less, so more vapour passes to the second stage. If that exceeds its design load, the second stage breaks and the first follows. When vacuum fails in summer, check cooling water temperature and flow and clean the condensers.

steps.q: Stripping solvent under vacuum. Why put a condenser before the vacuum pump?
steps.title: Condense first
steps.summary: Vapour at low pressure has a huge volume: 1 kg of toluene vapour at 50 mbar and 40 °C occupies about 6 m³, but condenses to about 1.2 litres of liquid. A condenser before the vacuum pump leaves the pump mostly air to handle, so it can be much smaller and the solvent is recovered. At 50 mbar toluene condenses at only about 30 °C, so use chilled water or brine in the condenser, and fit a catch pot before the pump.

opts.t: So the pump mostly sees air
To make the pump run faster

draw: chilled water or brine + catch pot

intro.text: Hi, I'm Bubbles. Today: vacuum. The pressure you can't see, and the leaks you can't find. Six questions. Ready?

outro-web.text: That's the lesson. Read more in the vacuum systems guide.

q1.text: Question 1. At sea level, the vacuum gauge reads −740 mmHg. What is the absolute pressure?

q1-r0.text: 740 absolute is barely a vacuum. That's a breeze, not a pull.

q1-r2.text: 1500? You added them. That's twice an atmosphere!

q1-r3.text: Negative absolute pressure? Even space can't do that.

q1-b0.text: A gauge measures against the air around it. At sea level that's about 760 millimetres of mercury.

q1-b1.text: The gauge counts down from the atmosphere. Minus 740 means 740 below it.

q1-b2.text: Absolute is atmosphere minus vacuum. 760 minus 740 leaves 20. That's about 27 millibar.

q1-b3.text: Up in the hills the air is thinner, so the same gauge reading means a different absolute pressure. Write vacuum in absolute units.

q2.text: Question 2. Isolated from the system, the pump pulls its normal vacuum on the same gauge. Where is the problem?

q2-r0.text: The pump just proved itself. Leave the poor thing alone.

q2-r1.text: Yes! The pump's fine. The system is the culprit.

q2-r2.text: Same gauge read fine on the pump. It's not lying.

q2-r3.text: The pump runs fine on its own. The power is fine.

q2-b0.text: Close the valve between the pump and the system, and watch the gauge on the pump side of the valve.

q2-b1.text: If the pump alone pulls down fine, the pump is healthy. The trouble is upstream.

q2-b2.text: Either air is leaking in, or something is giving off vapour: wet product, solvent in the lines, a warm condenser.

q2-b3.text: The next question tells you which one.

q3.text: Question 3. You isolate the system and watch the pressure rise. How do you tell a leak from vapour?

q3-r0.text: They look quite different, if you plot them. Grab a pen.

q3-r1.text: Exactly. Straight line, leak. Flattening curve, vapour.

q3-r2.text: Other way round. Air from outside never runs out.

q3-r3.text: Drop? Vapour coming off adds pressure. It doesn't take it away.

q3-b0.text: Pull down, shut the vacuum valve, and log the pressure every minute.

q3-b1.text: Air leaking in keeps coming at the same rate. The pressure climbs in a straight line.

q3-b2.text: Vapour stops coming once the space reaches the liquid's vapour pressure. The curve flattens.

q3-b3.text: For air near room temperature, the leak in kilograms an hour is about 0.07 times the volume in cubic metres times the rise in millibar per minute. Two cubic metres rising 10 millibar in 10 minutes is about 0.14 kilograms an hour.

q4.text: Question 4. The motive steam pressure to an ejector falls below design. What happens?

q4-r0.text: Improves with less push? Ejectors don't work on hope.

q4-r1.text: Yes! It breaks. Not gently, either.

q4-r3.text: Lower pressure, less steam through the nozzle. And worse vacuum.

q4-b0.text: An ejector has no moving parts. Steam shoots through a nozzle and drags the gas from the suction along with it.

q4-b1.text: Then it squeezes the mix up to the discharge pressure. That takes the full design steam pressure.

q4-b2.text: Drop much below it, and the ejector doesn't just get a bit weaker. It breaks, and the vacuum falls off suddenly.

q4-b3.text: Keep the motive steam at or slightly above design, and dry. Wet steam erodes the nozzle.

q5.text: Question 5. Summer. The inter-condenser cooling water runs warmer. What happens to a two-stage ejector?

q5-r0.text: Nothing? Your vacuum log disagrees every June.

q5-r1.text: Warmer water improving vacuum? Bubbles laughed so hard he popped.

q5-r2.text: Correct! More vapour slips through to the second stage.

q5-r3.text: Cooling water doesn't touch the steam header.

q5-b0.text: Between the stages, a condenser turns the steam and process vapour into liquid. The second stage only handles what's left.

q5-b1.text: Warmer water condenses less. More vapour goes on to the second stage.

q5-b2.text: If that's more than the second stage was sized for, the inter-condenser pressure rises, and the first stage breaks too.

q5-b3.text: So when vacuum fails in summer, check the cooling water temperature and flow, and clean the condensers.

q6.text: Question 6. Stripping solvent under vacuum. Why put a condenser before the vacuum pump?

q6-r0.text: The gauge will be fine. Think about the pump.

q6-r1.text: Yes! Let the condenser do the heavy lifting.

q6-r2.text: The pump runs at the same speed. It just has less to do.

q6-r3.text: Heat it? A condenser does the exact opposite.

q6-b0.text: Vapour at low pressure takes up a huge volume. One kilogram of toluene vapour at 50 millibar and 40 degrees fills about 6 cubic metres.

q6-b1.text: Condense it, and it shrinks to just over a litre of liquid.

q6-b2.text: Then the pump only handles the air and what's left. It can be much smaller, and you get the solvent back.

q6-b3.text: At 50 millibar toluene condenses at only about 30 degrees, so use chilled water or brine, and fit a catch pot before the pump. More in the vacuum systems guide on pharmacheme dot in.
